entries.name: receiver-type-none-over-filter-tx#0
entries.description: sigmaProp(Filter(1, (x: Int) => true).none[Int].isDefined) — a PropertyCall to SGlobal.none (method 10, one explicit type argument T = SInt, the trailing `04`) whose RECEIVER is a Filter over an Int. The explicit-type branch reads one type after the object and never reads the object's own type, so the ill-typed receiver is invisible: the tree PARSES. (The spend would fail at eval — `none`'s invoke needs a Global receiver — which the wire tier does not reach.) The same tree as a transaction's only output: a refusal here costs the whole transaction, not one box.

entries.name: receiver-type-getreg-propcall-tx#1
entries.description: sigmaProp(SELF.getReg[Int].isDefined) written as a ZERO-ARGUMENT PropertyCall (`a7` is SELF, `04` is T = SInt) — the same branch with a well-typed receiver, the type byte read. The positive control for the branch itself: an implementation that refuses this refuses the branch, not the receiver. (Eval throws on arity — getReg takes a register index.) The same tree as a transaction's only output: a refusal here costs the whole transaction, not one box.

entries.name: receiver-type-indices-over-filter-tx#2
entries.description: CONTROL sigmaProp(Filter(1, (x: Int) => true).indices.size == 0) — `SCollection.indices` (method 14) as a PropertyCall with NO explicit type arguments, over the SAME receiver as the first entry. Parse takes the other branch, `specializeFor(obj.tpe, …)` READS the receiver's type, and `Filter.tpe` casts SInt to SCollection: a ClassCastException, not a ValidationException, so the size bit does NOT degrade it. REJECTED outright. Both sides should agree here — it is what separates the two branches. The same tree as a transaction's only output: a refusal here costs the whole transaction, not one box.
